quote: I know they told me I had to have a tree removed.
stewart_read: Customer discloses a prior Ion touch and a specific stated DQ reason (tree/shading) but the rep never asks what company/rep said this or gathers detail — he moves straight to reframing without confirming the facts of the prior call.
alternative_hypothesis: Rep may have already known this was a repeat Ion touch (not a competitor) and judged the detail unnecessary since he had the address in front of him.
coaching_implication: Coach the rep to spend 10 seconds confirming what exactly was said in the prior call before deciding how to reframe — here it worked out, but the rep was guessing.

quote: Would you be willing to trim the tree? Like, trim that a little bit?
stewart_read: Rather than flipping the shading/tree objection into an urgency point (e.g., reframing the tree as secondary to the estimate itself), the rep negotiates directly on the customer's terms, which the customer then re-escalates back toward removal.
alternative_hypothesis: The direct negotiation was reasonable given this is a physical/structural constraint, not a cost objection — inversion framing may not map cleanly onto a shading DQ.
coaching_implication: This is a borderline case; flag it for discussion but don't over-coach — the physical objection type limits how much the inversion move applies.

quote: The last couple of months have been, like, $500.
stewart_read: This is a strong bill figure delivered with emphasis ('Oh, lord' from the rep just before), but the rep's only response is 'Oh, yeah. We can definitely help with that,' and the number is never referenced again — no flip into emotional alignment-against-the-utility, no callback at booking.
coaching_implication: Coach the rep to reflect the number back later — e.g., referencing the $500 bill when setting the appointment or in the confirmation text — to keep the pain anchored through to the closer.

quote: I'm not gonna lie to you. I don't even I don't need to even know the the usage. I just need to get a picture of it on that graph
stewart_read: Rep explicitly disclaims needing the usage number himself, which forfeits the chance to verbally anchor the bill pain in the moment — he is treating bill collection as pure data logistics rather than a conversational lever.
alternative_hypothesis: Strategically, deferring detailed usage analysis to the specialist is correct scope discipline — the miss is not deferring analysis, it's failing to verbally re-anchor the pain while capturing the photo.
coaching_implication: Show the rep the difference between 'I don't need the usage' (fine, scope-appropriate) and using the moment to say something like 'that graph's gonna back up what you told me about the $500 bills' — small verbal anchor costs nothing.

quote: And you you you so sure if that's it?
stewart_read: The bill-photo exchange visibly drags from roughly 03:23 to 08:10 with repeated failed sends, and the rep never pivots to a verbal read-back despite the schema's explicit 2-minute pivot guidance for exactly this friction type.
alternative_hypothesis: The rep may have judged the customer was close to success each time (a text 'about to send') and continuing was the shorter path versus resetting to verbal read-back.
coaching_implication: This is the clearest efficiency miss on the call — coach the 2-minute pivot rule explicitly: after ~2 failed send attempts, ask the customer to read the kWh number off the bill directly.

quote: Yeah. Well, I love to all find you a good time.
stewart_read: The eventual booking at 08:13-08:39 lands a day and a time (Monday 3PM) but skips the hour-block statement, the no-driving/computer instruction, and the 'is that fair?' handshake entirely — it closes on 'Okay. You have a great day' with no explicit recap.
coaching_implication: Walk the rep through the full button-up checklist — this call has a real date/time but the appointment is structurally thin and more vulnerable to no-show without the handshake and expectation-setting language.
